paragraphs: (a) Chapter 3 of Avot. In the Mishnah: Berakhot 5:5; Sotah 9:15.

(b) Derekh Chayyim, chapter 3 of Avot, is uncertain whether his father Dosa is the ben Harkinas mentioned there consecutively: first the son's words, R. Chanina ben Dosa, and then the father's, R. Dosa ben Harkinas. Although this one is “ben Dosa” and that one “R. Dosa ben Harkinas,” this is common in the Talmud: sometimes a man is named without a title and sometimes as Rabbi or Rav. Yuchasin writes under R. Chanina bar Chama that he was a priest, and in Rabbenu Chananel's name that Chama was R. Chanina ben Dosa's son. If so, R. Chanina ben Dosa was a priest, but Rambam did not mention him in his enumeration of priests. In my opinion this is unlikely, since R. Chanina ben Dosa lived in R. Yochanan ben Zakkai's days, before the destruction, while Chama, R. Chanina's father, lived in Rabbi's days. Derekh Emunah, part 1, gate 3, writes that R. Chanina ben Dosa was a physician. Perhaps, according to the above, R. Chanina bar Chama was his grandson, likewise a physician, and received medical knowledge from his grandfather; see there.

(c) He was exceedingly pious, was accustomed to miracles, and his prayer was heard. Taanit, chapter 3, 24b, and Yoma 53b: he was walking along the road carrying a basket of salt on his head. Rain came. He said, “Master of the universe, the whole world is at ease, and Chanina is distressed.” The rain stopped. When he reached home, he said, “The whole world is distressed”—needing water for its fields—“and Chanina is at ease.” Rain came. Every day a heavenly voice goes forth: “The whole world is sustained for the sake of Chanina My son, while Chanina My son is satisfied with a kav of carobs from one Sabbath eve to the next”: there in Taanit; Berakhot 17b. Every Sabbath eve his wife would heat the oven and throw in something that made smoke, so the neighbors would think she was baking, out of shame because she had nothing to bake. She had a wicked neighbor who said, “I know she has nothing; I will go and see.” She knocked at the door. His wife was ashamed and entered a room. A miracle occurred: the oven was full of bread and the trough full of dough. The neighbor said, “Bring your bread paddle, for your bread is burning.” She replied, “I too went in to bring the paddle.” It was taught: she really did enter to bring the paddle, since she was accustomed to miracles. His wife told him to pray that they be given some of what is stored up for the righteous in the world to come. He prayed; something like the palm of a hand emerged and gave him one leg of a golden table. He saw in a dream that the righteous would eat at three-legged tables, while he would eat at a two-legged table. He asked her, “Are you content that we eat at a table with one leg taken away?” She said, “Pray that they take it back.” He prayed, and they took it. It was taught: the latter miracle was greater than the first, for we have a tradition that heaven gives but does not take back. One day at twilight he saw his daughter distressed: she had mistaken vinegar for oil and put it in the lamp. He told her, “He who told oil to burn will tell vinegar to burn.” It burned all day, until they took light from it for havdalah. He had goats, and people told him, “Your goats cause damage,” eating vegetables in others' gardens. He answered, “If they cause damage, let bears eat them; if not, let each bring a bear on its horns.” In the evening each came with a bear on its horns. His neighbor built a house, but its beams did not reach. He asked her name. She said, “Ikku.” He said, “Ikku, let your beams reach.” Her beams reached. It was taught: Pelimo says, “I saw the house that R. Chanina ben Dosa roofed through his prayer; there was a cubit on this side and on that.” For the question of where he had goats from, etc., see Rashi in Ein Yaakov and Chiddushei Aggadot. Pesachim 112b: Igrat bat Machalat would go out with 180,000 destructive angels, each authorized to do harm once. Once R. Chanina ben Dosa met her. She said, “Were it not proclaimed in heaven, ‘Beware of Chanina My son and his Torah,’ I would make your blood worth two small coins.” He said, “If I am esteemed in heaven, I decree that you never pass through inhabited places.” She said, “Please leave me a little space.” He left her the nights that begin the Sabbath and Wednesday. Berakhot 34b: he prayed for the sick and said, “This one lives,” when his prayer flowed fluently from his mouth, and “This one dies.” He prayed for Rabban Gamliel's son. He went to study Torah with R. Yochanan ben Zakkai and prayed for his son. The daughter of Nechunya the well-digger (see there) fell into a pit; he said, “At this hour she has come up, etc.” Bava Batra 74b: that chest in the sea, into which his wife is destined to put fringes for the righteous in the future. Berakhot 33a; Jerusalem Talmud, Ein Omdin, end of mishnah 1: he killed an arod, and a spring opened beneath him. Had the arod reached water first, R. Chanina ben Dosa would have died. See Arukh, entry Chavarbar. The beginnings of Chazit Midrash and Kohelet Midrash relate that he wished to dedicate a stone to Jerusalem but had no money to pay for transporting it. Angels appeared and told him to lend them his hand; they set him down in Jerusalem. He sought to give them, etc.; see the story there. Demai, chapter 1, halakhah 3: R. Chanina ben Dosa sat to eat on Sabbath night, and the table sank away before him. They asked what this meant. He said, “I borrowed seasoning from my neighbor and did not tithe it.” He recalled the condition he had made before the Sabbath to separate it the next day, and the table rose by itself. Eruvin 53 and Shabbat 112b, near the end: if the earlier ones are sons of angels, we are sons of men; if they are sons of men, we are like donkeys, and not like the donkey of R. Pinchas ben Yair or R. Chanina ben Dosa. Rashi explains: R. Pinchas ben Yair's donkey is described in Chullin 7, and R. Chanina ben Dosa's in Taanit. End of quotation. But Taanit contains no such account of R. Chanina ben Dosa's donkey, only the goats mentioned above. I found in the new Talmud editions in Taanit another version: the donkey of R. Yosi of Yokrat. However, Avot DeRabbi Natan, end of chapter 8, has the story of R. Chanina ben Dosa's donkey being stolen and refusing to eat, etc. Jerusalem Demai, chapter 1, has the story of R. Pinchas ben Yair's donkey being stolen; see there. Shalshelet HaKabbalah, 27a, writes that Taanit, chapter 3, apparently indicates he eventually became wealthy. I do not know where this appears. Perhaps it refers to the golden table leg given him, but it is explicit that they took it back from him. Mishnah Sotah, end of Eglah Arufah, 49: when R. Chanina ben Dosa died, men of deed ceased.

(d) Yuchasin writes that he saw the Temple's destruction. R. Yeshayah, who fasted eighty-eight fasts to ask why the dog merited singing “Come, let us bow down” (see there), was his student. R. Chanina ben Dosa and his wife are buried at Araviyah: Gelilot Eretz Yisrael. And R. Reuven Itztrobuli.
